title: Ultrasonic distance sensor
desc: HC-SR04 measures distance, LED warns on proximity
content_html:
Materials

  • 1 x Arduino Uno (or Uno-compatible board) (Nerokas - nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x HC-SR04 Ultrasonic Distance Sensor module (Nerokas - nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x Breadboard (half-size or full-size) (Pixel Electronics - pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 1 x LED (5mm, any colour, red recommended for a "warning" light) (Pixel Electronics - pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 1 x 220Ω resistor (for the LED) (Nerokas - nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x Buzzer (optional, for an audible warning extension) (Pixel Electronics - pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 8 x Male-to-male jumper wires (Nerokas - nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x USB cable (A to B, for Arduino Uno) (Pixel Electronics - pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 1 x Laptop or computer with Arduino IDE installed (school-provided)
  • Optional: ruler or tape measure for calibration activity (school-provided)

How It Works

The HC-SR04 sensor works a lot like a bat finding its way in the dark, or a ship's sonar finding rocks underwater. It has two round "eyes" on the front — but they aren't eyes at all, they are a tiny speaker and a tiny microphone.

The speaker (called the Trigger) sends out a very short, very high-pitched sound — so high that humans cannot hear it. This sound travels through the air until it hits an object (a hand, a wall, a book) and bounces back, just like an echo in a canyon. The microphone (called the Echo) listens for that bounced-back sound.

The Arduino keeps track of exactly how long it took for the sound to leave and come back — this is measured in tiny fractions of a second called microseconds. Since we know how fast sound travels through air (about 343 metres per second), we can do some simple maths to turn "time taken" into "distance to the object." The Arduino does this maths for us every time it takes a reading.

Once the Arduino knows the distance, it makes a decision: if the object is closer than a distance we choose (say, 10cm), it turns on an LED to warn that something is too close — just like a reversing sensor in a car. This teaches an important programming idea: using sensor data to make decisions with an if statement.

Step-by-Step Instructions

  1. Introduce the HC-SR04 module to students. Point out its four pins: VCC, Trig, Echo, and GND. Explain that Trig "shouts" and Echo "listens."
  2. Place the HC-SR04 sensor on the breadboard (or hold it steady with wires — it does not need the breadboard if pins are used directly, but breadboard placement keeps wiring tidy).
  3. Wire the sensor: VCC to Arduino 5V, GND to Arduino GND, Trig to Arduino digital pin 9, Echo to Arduino digital pin 10.
  4. Insert the LED into the breadboard. Connect the LED's longer leg (anode) through the 220Ω resistor to Arduino digital pin 7. Connect the shorter leg (cathode) to a breadboard ground rail, then to Arduino GND.
  5. Double-check all wiring before connecting power — a wrong connection on the HC-SR04 will not usually damage it, but good habits matter.
  6. Connect the Arduino to the computer via USB. Open the Arduino IDE and paste in the sketch from the Full Code section below.
  7. Select the correct board (Arduino Uno) and correct COM port under the Tools menu.
  8. Upload the code. Open the Serial Monitor (set to 9600 baud) to see live distance readings printed in centimetres.
  9. Ask students to slowly move a hand towards the sensor while watching the Serial Monitor numbers decrease.
  10. Have students note the distance (in cm) at which the LED turns on. Ask them to guess this number before checking.
  11. Challenge students to change the threshold value in the code (e.g. from 10cm to 20cm) and re-upload to see the warning distance change.
  12. Wrap up by asking each group to explain, in their own words, how the sensor "sees" without eyes.

Full Code

// Ultrasonic Distance Sensor with LED Proximity Warning
// HC-SR04 measures distance; LED lights up when an object is too close

const int trigPin = 9;      // Pin connected to HC-SR04 Trig (sends the sound pulse)
const int echoPin = 10;     // Pin connected to HC-SR04 Echo (receives the bounced sound)
const int ledPin = 7;       // Pin connected to the warning LED

const int warningDistance = 10;  // Distance in cm below which the LED turns on

void setup() {
  pinMode(trigPin, OUTPUT);   // Trig sends a signal out, so it is an OUTPUT
  pinMode(echoPin, INPUT);    // Echo receives a signal, so it is an INPUT
  pinMode(ledPin, OUTPUT);    // LED is controlled by the Arduino, so it is an OUTPUT
  Serial.begin(9600);         // Start Serial communication so we can see readings on the computer
}

void loop() {
  // Step 1: Send a short pulse out of the Trig pin to trigger a measurement
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);   // Make sure Trig starts LOW (off)
  delayMicroseconds(2);         // Tiny pause to ensure a clean signal
  digitalWrite(trigPin, HIGH);  // Send the ultrasonic "shout"
  delayMicroseconds(10);        // Pulse must be at least 10 microseconds long
  digitalWrite(trigPin, LOW);   // Turn the trigger off again

  // Step 2: Measure how long the Echo pin stays HIGH
  // pulseIn() waits for the pin to go HIGH, then times how long it stays HIGH (in microseconds)
  long duration = pulseIn(echoPin, HIGH);

  // Step 3: Convert the time into a distance
  // Sound travels about 0.0343 cm per microsecond
  // We divide by 2 because the sound travels to the object AND back
  float distanceCm = (duration * 0.0343) / 2;

  // Step 4: Print the distance so we can see it on the Serial Monitor
  Serial.print("Distance: ");
  Serial.print(distanceCm);
  Serial.println(" cm");

  // Step 5: Decide whether to warn with the LED
  if (distanceCm > 0 && distanceCm < warningDistance) {
    // distanceCm > 0 filters out invalid/zero readings from sensor errors
    digitalWrite(ledPin, HIGH);  // Object too close - turn LED on
  } else {
    digitalWrite(ledPin, LOW);   // Object far away - turn LED off
  }

  delay(200);  // Small pause between readings so numbers don't scroll too fast to read
}

Common Mistakes & Fixes

SymptomLikely CauseFix
Serial Monitor shows "0.00 cm" constantly, or numbers that never changeTrig and Echo pins swapped, or wires loose in breadboardDouble-check wiring: Trig to pin 9, Echo to pin 10. Push wires firmly into breadboard holes.
LED never lights up even when an object is very closeLED inserted backwards (wrong polarity), or warningDistance value not matched to test distanceFlip the LED so the longer leg (anode) faces the resistor/pin side. Try moving object closer than the warningDistance value in code.
Readings jump wildly or show huge/impossible numbers (e.g. 400+ cm indoors)Sensor pointed at a soft, angled, or sound-absorbing surface (like fabric), or nothing in rangePoint sensor at a flat, hard surface directly in front of it, within 2cm-400cm range.
Nothing appears in Serial Monitor at allWrong baud rate selected in Serial Monitor, or Serial.begin() missing from codeSet Serial Monitor dropdown to 9600 baud to match Serial.begin(9600) in the sketch.
LED stays on permanently regardless of distanceLED wired directly to 5V instead of the Arduino pin, or code logic reversedConfirm LED anode connects to pin 7 (through resistor), not directly to 5V or GND.
Code uploads but Arduino resets repeatedly or acts erraticallyHC-SR04 drawing too much current, or loose USB connectionEnsure sensor VCC connects to 5V (not 3.3V), and USB cable is fully seated.

Discussion Questions

  • What two things does the HC-SR04 sensor actually have instead of "eyes," and what does each one do?
  • Why do we divide the total travel time by 2 when calculating distance?
  • Can you think of a real-world device that uses the same idea as this sensor (hint: bats, ships, parking sensors)?
  • What happens to the LED if you point the sensor at a soft object like a jersey compared to a hard object like a book? Why might that be?
  • If you wanted the warning to happen further away (say, 50cm instead of 10cm), which single line of code would you change?

Extension Challenges

  • Easy: Change the warning distance from 10cm to 30cm and confirm the LED now triggers earlier. Test with a ruler to measure exactly where it turns on.
  • Medium: Add a second LED (e.g. green) that stays on when the object is far away (safe), so you now have a green "safe" light and a red "warning" light working together based on distance.
  • Hard: Add a buzzer that beeps faster and faster as an object gets closer, using the distance value to control the delay between beeps (a real parking-sensor effect). Use the distanceCm variable to calculate the beep delay.
